blurb: From the covenant traditions of ancient Israel through Temple, exile, and rabbinic Judaism to the modern State of Israel — one God, Torah, and a people bound by law and memory.

events.description: The Torah's narratives of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — covenant, the promise of land, and one God — are set in the early 2nd millennium BCE; their historicity is a matter of faith and scholarly debate, not settled record.
events.title: Covenant traditions of the patriarchs

events.description: The story of Moses leading Israel out of slavery in Egypt and receiving the Law at Sinai. A 13th-century BCE setting is traditional; direct archaeological evidence for the event as narrated is lacking.
events.title: The Exodus tradition

events.description: A law book 'found' in the Temple (2 Kings 22) drives King Josiah's centralizing reform; scholars widely link it to the core of Deuteronomy, among the Torah's youngest layers.
events.title: Deuteronomy & Josiah's reform

events.description: Jerusalem falls to Babylon (586 BCE) and Judah's elite are deported; in exile, the prophet of Isaiah 40–55 proclaims an uncompromising monotheism and the hope of return.
events.title: Exile in Babylon & Second Isaiah

events.description: With Persian permission, exiles return and rebuild the Jerusalem Temple (dedicated 515 BCE), reorganizing Jewish life around Temple, Torah, and priesthood.
events.title: Return & the Second Temple

events.description: Tradition credits Ezra the scribe with publicly reading and enforcing the Torah in Persian-era Jerusalem — a landmark in Torah becoming the community's constitution. Which Artaxerxes he served is debated.
events.title: Ezra reads the Torah

events.description: Judah Maccabee's revolt against Seleucid religious persecution retakes and rededicates the Temple — the origin of Hanukkah — and wins a century of Hasmonean independence.
events.title: Maccabean revolt & Hanukkah

events.description: A sectarian community at Qumran copies and composes scriptures — including the oldest surviving biblical manuscripts — amid apocalyptic expectation under Roman rule.
events.title: Qumran & the Dead Sea Scrolls

events.description: After the Jewish revolt, Roman forces burn the Temple in 70 CE. Sacrificial worship ends permanently; rabbinic Judaism, centered on prayer, study, and synagogue, takes shape in its place.
events.title: Rome destroys the Second Temple

events.description: Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi compiles the Mishnah in Galilee: the first major written code of the oral Torah — civil, ritual, agricultural, and festival law organized by topic.
events.title: Mishnah compiled

events.description: Generations of Babylonian rabbis' debate around the Mishnah are redacted into the Talmud — ever since, the central text of rabbinic Judaism.
events.title: Babylonian Talmud completed

events.description: Moses Maimonides completes the Mishneh Torah, a complete code of Jewish law, and the Guide for the Perplexed, an attempt to reconcile Torah with Aristotelian philosophy.
events.title: Maimonides codifies & philosophizes

events.description: From the First Zionist Congress (1897) and the Balfour Declaration (1917) to the founding of Israel in 1948, political Zionism returns a Jewish state to the center of Jewish history.
events.title: Zionism & the State of Israel

name: Judaism
